extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with Wikipedia passages. It is designed to test entailment-like inference and answer questions with "yes" or "no".
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine, heuristically filtered for likely yes/no questions, then paired with a Wikipedia page and annotated by humans in a three-step process to identify a good question, a passage containing enough information, and the yes/no answer.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Questions were marked as “not answerable” if the Wikipedia article did not contain the requested information.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated Google search queries, Wikipedia pages/articles, and selected passages from those articles.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples; if there was a disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement. The resulting labels were treated as gold-standard labels. The paper also notes that they elected to use singly-annotated examples in the training/dev/test sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was assessed by comparing answer annotations against gold-standard labels created by author agreement; on 110 selected examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy. Disagreements were analyzed as six ambiguous/debatable cases and five annotator misunderstandings.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Three authors labeled each of the 110 randomly chosen examples for the quality check; the final dataset used singly-annotated examples.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: The annotators were authors of the paper.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was split into train/dev/test sets, with questions from NQ kept in the train set; additionally, only questions marked as having a yes/no answer were used, and each question was paired with a selected passage instead of the entire document.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated Google search queries, heuristically filtered to likely yes/no questions using indicator words and sufficient length, kept only if a Wikipedia page appeared in the first five results, and then annotated by humans who first judged question quality, found an answer-containing passage, and labeled the answer yes/no.

name.evidence: We build a reading comprehension dataset, BoolQ, of such questions

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: We split these questions into a 3.2k dev set, 3.2k test set, and 9.4k train set, ensuring questions from NQ are always in the train set. ... Note that, unlike in NQ, we only use questions that were marked as having a yes/no answer, and pair each question with the selected passage instead of the entire document.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries that are likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified: we found selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length, to be effective. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results... Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process. First, they decide if the question is good... Next, for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question. Finally, annotators mark whether the question’s answer is “yes” or “no”.
